claims.text: The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a near-equimolar composition and random atomic arrangement.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depends on particle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower thermal conductivity than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit greater thermal expansion than larger nanoparticles.
The size-dependent response arises because surface-to-volume ratio alters local vibrational dynamics.
Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to investigate the thermal response of HEA nanoparticles.
In-situ heating can be used to observe the thermal response and structural evolution of HEA nanoparticles.
A temperature range extending from room temperature to approximately 1000–1300 K is suitable for the proposed thermal study.
Nanoparticle diameters from approximately 3 nm to 20 nm form an appropriate size range for testing the predicted trend.
Changing surface-to-volume ratio modifies the vibrational density of states at nanoparticle surfaces.
Changing surface-to-volume ratio modifies surface atomic coordination.
A larger fraction of atoms are at or near the surface in smaller nanoparticles.
The larger surface-atom fraction in smaller nanoparticles enhances atomic vibrations and modifies phonon transport.
Enhanced atomic vibrations increase thermal expansion in smaller nanoparticles.
Modified vibrational behavior can reduce effective thermal conductivity.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk material provide a baseline with a lower surface-to-volume ratio.
High-temperature coalescence or sintering may obscure nanoparticle size-dependent effects.
High-temperature structural evolution may obscure the proposed size-dependent effects.
Limitations of interatomic potentials make the magnitude of the predicted response uncertain.
The hypothesis is falsified if smaller nanoparticles do not systematically show both lower thermal conductivity and higher thermal expansion under otherwise identical conditions.
